chief_complaint: severe nausea and vomiting in early pregnancy, unable to keep fluids down
hpi_details: 28F who is 8 weeks pregnant presents with severe, persistent nausea and vomiting. Reports vomiting 5-6 times daily, unable to keep food or water down for 24 hours, and feeling extremely weak.
ideas: worried about the health of her baby due to constant vomiting
expectations: wants anti-nausea medication and IV fluids

investigation_events.title: Urgent dehydration and electrolyte assessment
investigation_events.availability_message: Urine ketone and electrolyte results are now available. IV fluids and thiamine should not be delayed in this clinically dehydrated patient.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Hyperemesis gravidarum is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes Evidence-based diagnostic and therapeutic protocol for Hyperemesis Gravidarum (severe pregnancy-induced nausea/vomiting causing dehydration), adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: severe nausea and vomiting in early pregnancy, unable to keep fluids down

Key HPI features: 28F who is 8 weeks pregnant presents with severe, persistent nausea and vomiting. Reports vomiting 5-6 times daily, unable to keep food or water down for 24 hours, and feeling extremely weak.

Objective/Exam findings: Complete vital signs and focused physical examination required. Diagnostic workup tailored for Hyperemesis Gravidarum (severe pregnancy-induced nausea/vomiting causing dehydration).
Relevant background/PMH: Primigravida (8 weeks gestation by LMP)
Current medications: Prenatal vitamins (stopped due to nausea)
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Hyperemesis gravidarum.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Normal nausea/vomiting of pregnancy without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Unable to tolerate any fluids for 24 hours.
management_principles: Evidence-based diagnostic and therapeutic protocol for Hyperemesis Gravidarum (severe pregnancy-induced nausea/vomiting causing dehydration)
Check weight loss, vital signs for orthostasis, urine ketones, and electrolytes
Administer IV fluids with thiamine, and prescribe antiemetics (Pyridoxine/Doxylamine first line)
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

teaching.one_liner: 28F at 8 weeks with severe persistent vomiting, unable to tolerate oral intake for 24 hours.
red_flags: Unable to tolerate any fluids for 24 hours

must_ask.say: How many times have you vomited today, and can you keep anything down?
Have you felt weak, dizzy, or had a dry mouth?

must_ask.objective: Ask about weight and appetite changes
must_ask.say: Have you lost weight since the vomiting started?
How has this been affecting you emotionally, and do you have support at home?

must_ask.objective: Explain IV fluids and antiemetic plan
must_ask.say: We'll start IV fluids and give you medication to control the nausea.

history.answer: I am 8 weeks pregnant, and I haven't been able to keep any food or water down for the past 24 hours because of constant nausea and vomiting.
The nausea began mildly around 6 weeks, but it worsened sharply over the past week and became unbearable yesterday.
I am throwing up 5 to 6 times every day, even when my stomach is completely empty.
At first it was undigested food, but now it is mostly clear fluid or bitter, yellowish-green bile without blood or foul odor.
The nausea lasts all day and night rather than just mornings, and the vomiting is not shooting out forcefully.
I do not have severe stomach pain, just some mild aching in my upper belly after dry heaving that eases up afterward.
I passed gas today and had a normal bowel movement two days ago with no diarrhea, and my belly does not feel bloated.
I have had no fever or chills, and my husband ate the same food as me without any sickness.
I feel lightheaded when standing up, but I have had no headache, stiff neck, blurry vision, or confusion.
No, I have not bumped or injured my head recently.
I throw up even tiny sips of water, my mouth is parched, and I have only urinated once today and it was very dark.
My mouth feels dry, but I have not had excessive urination or extreme thirst prior to this, and I do not have diabetes.
No, I do not have any chest pain, tightness, or shortness of breath.
I do not drink alcohol, smoke marijuana, or use any recreational drugs.
I have lost about 3 kilograms over the past two weeks because I cannot keep meals down.
My appetite is completely gone, and even the smell of cooking makes me violently nauseous.
No, I never induce vomiting myself. It happens completely involuntarily.
No, I have not had any vaginal bleeding, spotting, or unusual discharge.
I feel utterly drained and overwhelmed, though my husband is being very supportive and brought me to the clinic today.
I know morning sickness happens, but I am terrified that not keeping any fluids or food down will harm my baby.
I feel completely exhausted, dehydrated, and weak, and I am worried my body cannot take much more of this.
I am hoping I can get IV fluids to rehydrate me and medication that will safely stop the vomiting.
I have no chronic medical conditions and have always been healthy.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been hospitalized.
I was taking prenatal vitamins, but I had to stop taking them a few days ago because they made my nausea worse.
I have no known allergies to medications or foods.
I have never smoked cigarettes.
I do not drink alcohol at all, especially now that I am pregnant.
I work in an office at a desk job and live with my husband in an apartment.
My mother had severe morning sickness during her pregnancies, but there is no family history of gastrointestinal or metabolic diseases.
My last menstrual period was 8 weeks ago, my cycles were regular every 28 days, and this is my first pregnancy.
This was a planned and very wanted pregnancy, and we stopped using barrier contraception several months ago.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 100/65 mmHg, pulse rate 104 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, body temperature 36.8°C.
Standing blood pressure drops to 88/55 mmHg and pulse increases to 122 beats per minute, consistent with orthostatic hypotension.
Lethargic and visibly fatigued young woman with sunken eyes and dry lips.
Oral mucous membranes are dry with a cracked tongue; pharynx is clear without erythema or exudate.
Decreased skin turgor with delayed recoil on the forearm; capillary refill time is prolonged at 3 seconds.
Thyroid gland is normal in size, non-tender, with no palpable nodules or bruits.
Abdomen is flat and non-distended with no surgical scars or visible pulsations.
Bowel sounds are present and normoactive in all four quadrants.
Abdomen is soft throughout with no rigidity or guarding; mild epigastric discomfort on deep palpation without focal tenderness.
No rebound tenderness in any quadrant.
Neck is supple with negative Kernig and Brudzinski signs.
No spontaneous, gaze-evoked, or positional nystagmus.
Alert and oriented to time, place, and person, but responds slowly due to exhaustion.
